topic: Generics & variance: in, out & star projection

questions.question: Which line fails to compile, and why?
options: Line 3: a `val` cannot point to an object that another `val` already points to
Line 1: `mutableListOf` returns a read-only list unless its type argument is written out explicitly
Line 2: `List` is invariant too, so a `List<String>` can never be assigned to a `List<Any>`
Line 3: `MutableList` is invariant, or you could add an `Int` to a list of strings through `mutable`
questions.explanation: `List<out E>` is covariant because it only produces values, so `List<String>` is a `List<Any>`. `MutableList<E>` both reads and writes `E`, so it is invariant. If line 3 were allowed, `mutable.add(42)` would put an Int into a list that `strings` still treats as strings.

questions.question: For `interface Producer<out T> { fun get(): T }`, a `Producer<String>` can be used where a `Producer<Any>` is expected.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `out T` means `T` only appears in output positions, so anything you can get from a `Producer<String>` is also an `Any`. That makes `Producer<String>` a subtype of `Producer<Any>`. The compiler enforces this by rejecting `T` as a parameter type of public members.

questions.question: `sortedWith` on a `List<String>` takes a `Comparator<in String>`. Why can you pass a `Comparator<Any>` that compares by `hashCode()`?
options: `String` implements `Comparable`, so the compiler converts the `Comparator<Any>` to a `Comparator<String>`
Comparators are erased at runtime, so the compiler allows any comparator for any element type
`Any` is a supertype of `String`, and every generic type follows the subtype relation of its type argument
`in T` makes Comparator contravariant: what can compare two `Any` values can compare two strings
questions.explanation: A comparator only consumes values, so it is declared `Comparator<in T>`. Contravariance flips the subtyping: `Comparator<Any>` is a subtype of `Comparator<String>`. Generic types are not covariant by default, so 'every generic type follows its argument' is wrong; it depends on the declared variance.

questions.question: What does this print?
options:
9
apple

9
pear

9
fig

4
fig
questions.explanation: The bound `T : Comparable<T>` lets the function compare values of any comparable type. For Ints the largest is 9. Strings compare alphabetically, so "pear" is greater than "fig" and "apple"; it is not about length or position.

questions.question: Given `val list: MutableList<*> = mutableListOf("a", "b")`, which lines compile? Select all that apply.
options: `list.add(null)`
`list.add("c")`
`val x: Any? = list[0]`
`list.clear()`
`val s: String = list[0]`
questions.explanation: `MutableList<*>` means a list of some unknown type. Reading is safe as `Any?`, and members that do not mention the type parameter, like `clear()` or `size`, work. Writing is blocked because the unknown type could be anything, so even `null` cannot be added. Reading as `String` needs an explicit cast.

questions.question: Why does this class not compile?
options: A `var` has a setter taking `T`, which is an `in` position, so `T` can't be declared `out`
Type parameters declared `out` cannot appear in any constructor parameter, `val` or `var`
A covariant type parameter must always have an upper bound such as `T : Any`
`out` can only be used on type parameters of interfaces, never on those of classes
questions.explanation: `out T` promises that `T` is only produced, never consumed. A `var` generates a setter `set(value: T)`, which consumes `T`, so the compiler rejects it. Making it `val` fixes the problem: constructor parameters are not variance-checked, and a `val` only adds a getter, which is an out position.

questions.question: What does this print?
options:
cast ok, size 2
CCE
CCE

cast ok, size 2
1

cast ok, size 1
CCE
questions.explanation: Type arguments are erased, so the cast to `List<String>` only checks that the object is a `List` and succeeds. The failure happens later, when `strs[1]` is used as a `String` and the compiler's hidden cast meets an `Int`. Unchecked casts move the error far away from the code that caused it.

questions.question: What does this signature require of `T`?
questions.code: fun <T> process(x: T) where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { }
options: `T` must be both a `CharSequence` and `Comparable<T>`
`T` must be either a `CharSequence` or a `Comparable<T>`
`T` must be a subclass of a class that implements both types
`T` must be a `CharSequence`, and the `Comparable` bound is only checked at runtime
questions.explanation: A `where` clause lists several upper bounds, and the type argument must satisfy all of them. `String` works because it is both a `CharSequence` and a `Comparable<String>`. Kotlin has no 'either' bounds, and all bounds are checked at compile time.

questions.question: Why can `Loading` be returned from a function whose return type is `Result<User>`?
options: The compiler infers `Loading` as `Result<User>` at each use, because its type argument is not fixed
`object` declarations are compatible with every type argument of their sealed parent
`Nothing` is erased to `Object` at runtime, so the JVM accepts it for any type argument
`Nothing` is a subtype of `User`, and `out T` makes `Result<Nothing>` a subtype of `Result<User>`
questions.explanation: `Nothing` is a subtype of every type, and because `Result` is covariant, `Result<Nothing>` is a subtype of `Result<T>` for any `T`. That lets a single `Loading` object serve every `Result<T>`. If `Result` were invariant (no `out`), this would not compile.
